interviewQuestions.question: What problem does HTTP/2 solve compared to HTTP/1.1, and how?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it around head-of-line (HOL) blocking, because that's the actual root cause HTTP/2 was built to remove. HTTP/1.1 processes requests on a connection strictly one at a time by default — a slow response at the front of the queue blocks every request behind it, even ones the server could have answered instantly. Browsers worked around this by opening roughly 6 parallel TCP connections per host, but that's a patch, not a fix: each connection still pays its own TCP handshake (and TLS handshake over HTTPS) cost, and you're now competing for bandwidth across multiple connections instead of using one efficiently.

HTTP/2 fixes the actual cause rather than working around the symptom. It introduces a **binary framing layer**: every message gets chopped into frames, each tagged with a **stream ID**, and a single TCP connection carries many streams' frames interleaved — the server can send stream 3's response frames between stream 1's, and the client reassembles each stream by ID on arrival. One slow response no longer blocks unrelated ones sharing the connection, and there's no need for multiple parallel connections at all, so the handshake cost is paid once, not six times.

On top of multiplexing, HTTP/2 adds **HPACK** header compression (covered in more depth elsewhere) and lets the server assign relative **stream priorities**, so a browser can hint "this CSS file matters more than this analytics beacon" and the server can schedule accordingly — genuinely useful for a real page load with dozens of resources of varying importance.

**Testing:** whether you understand HOL blocking as the specific root cause HTTP/2 targets, not just "HTTP/2 is faster," and whether you can explain the actual framing mechanism rather than gesturing at 'multiplexing' as a buzzword.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What HTTP/2 fixes

interviewQuestions.question: Does HTTP/2 fully eliminate head-of-line blocking?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
No, and this is a common trap that separates surface familiarity from real understanding. HTTP/2 eliminates HOL blocking specifically at the **application layer** — many logical requests can be in flight on one connection simultaneously without queuing behind each other, which is the real, felt improvement over HTTP/1.1's strict serialization.

But HTTP/2 still runs over **TCP**, and TCP's core contract is that it delivers bytes to the application in strict sequential order, no exceptions. If a single TCP segment is lost anywhere in that stream, TCP won't hand *any* subsequent bytes to the application layer until the lost segment is retransmitted and arrives — even if those later bytes belong to a completely unrelated HTTP/2 stream that suffered no loss at all. From HTTP/2's point of view, every multiplexed stream on that connection stalls simultaneously, waiting on a retransmission for data that might belong to just one of them. This is genuinely a different, transport-layer instance of head-of-line blocking, and no amount of clever framing at the HTTP layer can fix it, because the blocking happens one layer below where HTTP/2 operates — TCP's ordering guarantee is unconditional and not something the application can opt out of per-stream.

This exact limitation is the direct motivation for QUIC: instead of trying to patch TCP's behavior, QUIC replaces it, running over UDP and reimplementing reliability and ordering **per stream** rather than per connection, so a loss on one stream only stalls that stream.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish which layer a given fix operates at, and specifically whether you can name TCP's in-order-delivery guarantee as the actual mechanism causing the residual blocking, not just assert that 'some blocking remains.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: HOL blocking isn't fully gone

interviewQuestions.question: What is HPACK and why does HTTP/2 need it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
HPACK is HTTP/2's dedicated header-compression scheme, and I'd explain why headers specifically need their own solution rather than just reusing general-purpose compression. Request headers — `Cookie`, `User-Agent`, the various `Accept-*` fields — repeat almost verbatim across every request a client makes to the same host, sometimes hundreds of bytes of near-identical text sent again and again. HTTP/1.1 has no mechanism to avoid this; it resends the full plaintext header block on every single request, which becomes real, measurable overhead once you count dozens of requests per page load, each carrying its own copy of the same cookie.

HPACK avoids gzip-style general compression deliberately — general compression over a stream of separate HTTP messages historically enabled the CRIME/BREACH class of attacks that exploit compression to leak secrets across message boundaries, so HTTP/2 needed a compression scheme designed with that constraint in mind. Instead, HPACK maintains a **static table** of extremely common header field/value pairs (baked into the spec itself, covering things like common `:method: GET` and standard content types) plus a **dynamic table** that both the client and server build up incrementally as a connection progresses, recording headers actually seen on this specific connection. Once a header has appeared once, subsequent occurrences can be sent as a tiny index reference into one of these tables instead of the full text, with Huffman coding applied to whatever text still needs to be sent literally (like a unique cookie value).

The practical payoff is real and connection-specific: a cookie sent in full on request one might be a single-byte index reference by request five, which meaningfully reduces the per-request overhead for header-heavy traffic — a distinct saving from body compression, which HPACK doesn't touch at all.

**Testing:** whether you know header overhead is a distinct problem from body size, why HPACK avoids generic stream compression specifically (the CRIME/BREACH lineage), and how the static/dynamic table mechanism actually achieves the saving.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: HPACK's purpose

interviewQuestions.question: Why was HTTP/2 server push mostly abandoned?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Server push let a server proactively send resources it expected the client would need next — pushing a page's CSS file alongside the HTML response, before the browser even parses the HTML far enough to discover it needs that CSS — theoretically saving a full round trip per pushed resource.

The idea failed in practice for a specific, informative reason: the server has no reliable way to know what the browser **already has cached**. A server pushing a CSS file the browser already cached from a previous visit isn't saving a round trip at all — it's wasting bandwidth sending bytes the client discards immediately, and worse, on a connection where bandwidth is genuinely scarce (mobile, congested networks), that wasted push can actively **delay** the resources the browser genuinely needs, competing for the same limited connection capacity. Getting the caching heuristics right turned out to be much harder than the spec's designers anticipated, and in measured practice, push frequently made real page loads slower rather than faster once cache hit rates were accounted for. Chrome formally dropped support for it in 2022, and other major browsers followed a similar path, effectively retiring the feature from the ecosystem despite it remaining technically part of the spec.

Most sites chasing the same underlying goal — start fetching a critical resource earlier — moved to **103 Early Hints** instead: the server sends a preliminary informational response containing `Link` headers suggesting what to preload, *before* the final response is ready, but critically the decision to actually fetch anything stays with the **browser**, which already knows its own cache state. That inversion of control — hint, don't push — is exactly what server push got backwards.

**Testing:** whether you know this real-world nuance (push is largely dead, and specifically why) rather than reciting the spec as if it's still a commonly deployed optimization, and whether you understand the caching-blindness problem that actually killed it.
